title: Parting with kindness
hook: even divorce comes with limits, a waiting period and kindness (65:1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: as much as you can. Mindful of Allah, at the size you actually are, not the size you wish you were. Did one thing get done at a real size? Day six hundred thirty-two.

Most endings are messy. A friendship goes quiet. A job ends with a badge handed back at a desk. A marriage ends with lawyers, or silence, or a slammed door. When things fall apart, people tend to drop their manners first. Now open the sixty-fifth surah of the Qur'an. Its name is at-Talaq, divorce. A whole chapter, named for an ending. And the first thing it does is slow everything down. Count the days. Don't push anyone out of the house. Bring witnesses. Be kind on the way out the door.

The surah opens by speaking to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and through him to everyone. When you divorce, it says, do it with regard to the waiting period, the 'iddah, and count it carefully. During that time, the verse says, don't turn the women out of their houses, and they shouldn't leave, except in a case of open indecency. Then a phrase the Qur'an uses in other places too: these are the limits of Allah, the hudud. And whoever oversteps them has wronged his own soul. At the end of verse one comes a quieter line. The Qur'an adds, in effect: you don't know, perhaps Allah will bring about something new after this. The waiting period isn't only paperwork. It's a pause. Two people living under one roof, still, with time to cool down, and maybe to change their minds. Verse two says what happens when the waiting is over. Either keep them in kindness, or part from them in kindness. The Arabic is bi-ma'ruf: in the way that's recognized as right, decent, fair. Both doors, staying and leaving, carry the same word. And bring two just witnesses, so nobody can later rewrite what happened. The schools of Islamic law work out the details differently, how the waiting is counted, whether the witnesses are required. But the shape is shared. Even the end of a marriage has limits. Even a parting has manners. The Qur'an doesn't pretend divorce never happens. It says that when it does, the person walking away still owes the other person decency.

The practice: end one thing gracefully. It doesn't have to be big. A conversation you keep cutting off. A group chat you've been ghosting. A habit, a commitment, a project that's done. Sit still and pick one. Then picture the ending you'd be glad to have given: a clear word, no slammed door, nothing taken that isn't yours. If an ending in your life was hard, let it be hard. Just notice what kindness would have looked like. The bell holds the time.
Parting with kindness. In at-Talaq, the end of a marriage has a waiting period, limits and witnesses, and staying or leaving both happen bi-ma'ruf, in kindness. Today's word.
Your line: part with kindness. Today, when you leave something, a room, a call, a conversation that went badly, leave it a little gentler than it would have been. Day six hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: In Islamic law divorce is permitted but hedged with rules: a waiting period ('iddah) during which, in a revocable divorce, the wife normally stays in the home, the option of reconciliation, witnesses, and the instruction that a couple either stay together or part bi-ma'ruf, in kindness. The schools of law differ on details.

myth: the Qur'an has a whole surah named for divorce
surah 65, at-Talaq, opens with the rules for it.
in 65:1 the wife must leave the house at once
the verse says not to turn her out during the waiting period.
the verse says perhaps something new will come after
the waiting period leaves room for a change of heart.

fork.setup: a marriage is ending. the waiting period has begun. by 65:1, where does the wife live while it runs?
options: she goes to her family by law.
fork.reveal: she stays. the verse forbids turning her out, and adds: perhaps Allah will bring about something new after this.

original.note: Arabic: in kindness, in the way recognized as right. 65:2 uses it for staying and for parting alike.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chapter of rules about divorce.
what it means: even an ending has limits: a waiting period, a home kept, witnesses, and kindness either way.
what a scholar hears: ma'ruf shares a root with 'urf, what people recognize as decent; the 'iddah also leaves room for return before it ends.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:229 (retain in kindness or release in kindness)
classical fiqh on the 'iddah and on witnesses to divorce

notes: 65:1–2 paraphrased throughout, not quoted; confirm the paraphrase of the waiting period, the 'open indecency' exception and 'perhaps Allah will bring about something new'.
The schools differ on whether two witnesses are required for the divorce itself (required in Shia Ja'fari law; generally recommended in Sunni schools). The script says only that they differ; confirm.
The practice touches on divorce gently; a Keeper may want to check tone for listeners who have been through one.
The trapdoor's link of ma'ruf to 'urf (custom) is a standard lexical point; confirm.

Reviewer softened howItsDone: the wife staying in the home during the 'iddah is tied to revocable divorce; schools differ on housing after an irrevocable divorce. The fork/myth answers rest on 65:1 as written; confirm they don't overstate the rule.
